site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: A Boatman's Gift Across the Ganga
body: When Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana reached the wide Ganga on their journey into exile, the boatman Kevata welcomed them with gentle hands and a ready smile. He asked no payment, only the quiet joy of serving those he admired.

Rama accepted the offering with warm gratitude, offering friendship in place of royal coin. The river flowed steady and slow as Kevata poled them across, his heart full that a simple ferry could become a worthy gift to the prince.

On the far bank they stepped ashore beneath a brightening sky, while Kevata watched them go with a glad and peaceful face. In that small crossing, service and kindness met, and the river carried them all gently forward into hope.

stories.title: Small Friends, Steady Hearts
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: Along a sun-warmed bough, an elephant's careless step scattered a sparrow's nest, leaving only broken shells and quiet grief. But the sparrow was not alone; her loyal friends, a woodpecker, a fly, and a frog, gathered close to share her sorrow and devise a plan woven from their separate gifts.

The fly buzzed softly at the great beast's ears until his eyes grew heavy and closed. Then the woodpecker pecked, and the elephant, maddened and thirsty, stumbled toward the frog's croaking beside a hidden pit. Mistaking the sound for water, he tumbled into the deep, while the small friends watched safely from the shade.

Together they proved what the sparrow had begun to believe: that thoughtful cooperation and steady companionship can meet even the heaviest strength with grace. In the dappled forest, her small heart lifted, knowing no loss is final when friends stand beside you.

stories.title: A Prince's Steady Heart
body: When young Prince Dhruva was told he could not sit on his father's lap, the words stung deeply. Rather than meet insult with anger, his mother Suniti counseled him to seek the Supreme Lord Vishnu himself, who welcomes every sincere soul.

Wandering into the quiet forest, Dhruva met the sage Narada, who bestowed a sacred mantra and patient guidance. The boy practiced with rare steadiness, easing his needs and fixing his thoughts in devotion until, at last, Vishnu appeared radiant before him.

Dhruva, forgetting the crown he once sought, offered only praise and received Vishnu's blessing. He returned home honored by his father, and ruled wisely for years to come, his childhood sorrow transformed into resilience and grace.

stories.title: Hanuman Brings the Healing Mountain
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda (Gita Press translation)
body: In the fierce battle for Lanka, Lakshmana fell gravely wounded by a powerful weapon, and the physician Sushena declared that only a life-restoring herb from a distant Himalayan peak could save him before dawn. Hearing this, Hanuman surged northward on his great leap, his heart set on his friend.

When he reached the mountain, the herb was nowhere to be found among its countless plants, and he would not return empty-handed to those he loved. With swift resolve, he lifted the entire peak itself, carrying it through the night sky toward the weary army camped beyond Lanka's burning walls.

Sushena quickly found the needed medicine, and Lakshmana rose recovered as the mountain's fragrance swept across the field, reviving many wounded vanaras. Rama embraced Hanuman in deep gratitude, and hope flooded the army once more, their rescue accomplished through devoted friendship and unwavering persistence.

stories.title: The Wise Merchant of the Wilderness
stories.source: Apannaka Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: Two merchant caravans prepared to cross a dangerous wilderness, the Bodhisatta leading one and a foolish merchant leading the other. When desert goblins disguised as travelers told the foolish leader that rain had flooded the road ahead, he believed them and cast away his water jars, dooming his people to perish from thirst.

The Bodhisatta, wise to the strangers' true nature as goblins, kept his own caravan’s supplies intact and traveled cautiously by night through the desert. Along the way, he discovered the abandoned goods left behind and gathered them to enrich his companions.

His prudent leadership preserved the whole caravan, reaching safety together with unexpected bounty. The story ends in hope, showing how patient wisdom and clear-eyed care can guide a community safely home.
